  "text": "By spring the harbour wall needed pointing. Men came with buckets and worked between tides. Maren passed them on her way to buy bread. One asked whether the lighthouse would ever be lit again.

She said she did not think so.

He nodded and pressed mortar into a gap. It pleased her that he had asked nothing else.

The evenings lengthened. Erris no longer waited on the wall every night. There were other girls, a bicycle with a bent wheel, business at the far end of the village. Sometimes Maren saw her running and had to look twice to recognise her without the stillness.

At the lighthouse, she opened the window that had been painted shut. It took a knife and most of an afternoon. Air moved through the lamp-room. Beneath the salt and old oil she could smell the wet earth of the headland.

That night she wound the clock. Then she sat at the little desk and turned back through her mother's entries.

Wind. Tide. Three turns.

Forty years, in a hand that grew smaller near the end.

Maren had brought a pencil. Below her own record she wrote: Bought bread. Opened north window.

She waited, listening. The clock went on.

There had been other things. A yellow flower growing from the harbour steps. Erris laughing with her head thrown back. She could put them in tomorrow, if she remembered.

Downstairs, the door caught on its sill. Maren lifted it and pulled it closed. She went home with the key in her pocket and flour still caught in the seam of her sleeve."

  "text": "In June, Erris brought supper to the lighthouse in a saucepan wrapped in a towel. She had made too much, she said, though there were exactly two pieces of fish.

They ate beside the open window. Below them, a man was trying to persuade his dog into a boat. His voice carried clearly across the water; the dog's objections did not require a voice.

Erris laughed. Maren steadied her plate on her knees.

When the girl had gone, the room seemed larger than before. Maren washed the forks in the little basin and left them on the sill. There was still an hour until the winding.

She took down an older volume of the log, looking for the date her mother had repaired the stair. Halfway through November, between a falling barometer and a report of weed choking the harbour mouth, she found a faint round stain. A cup had stood there. Beneath it, almost erased, were the words: M. home late. Kept soup.

Maren rested her thumb against the margin. She could not remember the evening. There had been so many evenings when she had come in cold and impatient, wanting something other than what was waiting.

At ten past twelve she climbed to the clock and gave the key its three turns.

In the new log she entered the wind, the tide, and the winding. Then she wrote: Erris brought fish. Must return saucepan.

She went downstairs carrying it. Outside, the boats shifted against their ropes, and somewhere along the dark quay a dog shook water from its coat."

  "text": "Erris's kitchen light was still on. Maren stood outside with the saucepan, suddenly embarrassed by the hour. Before she could leave it on the step, the door opened.

‘You needn't have washed it,’ Erris said.

‘I know.’

Neither moved. Behind Erris, bread dough rose beneath a cloth. A stocking hung from the oven rail, its heel turned outward for mending.

‘Come tomorrow,’ Erris said. ‘There'll be rolls.’

Maren almost explained about the morning readings. Instead she asked what time.

Walking back, she heard the lighthouse strike one. She counted without meaning to, then waited for a second stroke that did not come. The harbour lay where it should. Water lipped the lowest stair.

She slept badly, as she often did now that sleep was possible. Once she woke convinced she had forgotten the winding. Her palm still held the soreness of the key; she pressed it against the mattress until the room became her room again.

At seven she entered the readings. At eight she put on her good coat, although the weather was fine.

There was a space beneath the last entry. She considered writing where she was going, in case anyone came looking. But no one had needed such an account before, and she was only crossing the village.

She left the pen beside the book.

Outside Erris's house, flour dusted the sill. Maren raised her hand to knock and heard chairs being moved inside: one dragged across the flags, then another.

She waited, listening to the small domestic scrape, before she made herself heard."
